opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really interesting question, because ChatGPT is kind of a special thing. Most AI companies are model companies that also happen to have a product, but ChatGPT became a super app almost by accident. It started as a research demo, and then it became this default entry point where hundreds of millions of people go when they have any question or task.

That shapes the landscape in a few ways. First, anything that is very general, like a general assistant, general chat, or general search over knowledge, is hard for a startup to compete on, because the super app gets the default position. When the model gets better, ChatGPT gets better automatically. If your product is basically "ChatGPT but slightly different," you're in a tough spot.

But I don't think that means there's no room. A super app is optimized for the median user and the median task. It's broad, but it's not deep in any particular context. What I've been thinking about is that the next stage of AI is less about making the model smarter in the abstract and more about putting it in the right environment: the right context, the right tools, the right feedback loops. A general app can't own every context. If you go deep into a specific workflow, say a certain kind of professional work or coding, where the data, the interface, and the evaluation are very particular, you can build something the super app can't easily replicate. You're defining the task and the environment, not just wrapping the model.

The other thing is that a super app creates a kind of gravity, but it also educates the market. Before ChatGPT, people didn't know what to ask an AI to do. Now people have expectations, and they keep hitting the limits of what a general chat interface can do. Those limits are where opportunities come from. Chat is a great interface for some things, but for many tasks it's actually not the right form factor. A lot of value will come from people inventing new interaction paradigms rather than competing on the chat box.

So my view is that startups shouldn't think of it as "how do I beat ChatGPT," but "what does ChatGPT structurally not want to do, or can't do well because it has to serve everyone." That's usually depth, specific context, and a different interface. And honestly, the model companies also want an ecosystem. They can't build everything. The question is whether you're building something that gets stronger as the models get stronger, or something that gets eaten as the models get stronger. That's the most important test.

r001.rationale: The response describes how ChatGPT’s super app affects startup competition, but does not say that adopting a super app reorganizes a company’s activities around it.

r002.rationale: It identifies opportunities in going deep on specific workflows and contexts, using different interfaces, and building for what ChatGPT cannot do well—products with a substantially different approach from ChatGPT.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it reshapes opportunities a lot, but mostly not in the direction people assume.

Let me step back a bit. If you think about what ChatGPT actually is, it's the first product that turned a general-purpose language model into a consumer-scale distribution channel. Hundreds of millions of people now have a default place to go when they want to ask something, write something, or figure something out. That's a very different situation from, say, 2022, when a startup could win just by wrapping a model in a reasonable interface. That window is basically closed. If your product is "ChatGPT but for X," and X is something ChatGPT can do reasonably well in the chat box, you're competing against a super app with better models, more data, and a distribution advantage you can't match.

So the naive reading is that the super app crushes everyone. But I don't think that's right either, and the reason comes back to how I think about agents. An agent is really defined by its environment and its tools, not by the model alone. ChatGPT, as a product, lives in a very specific environment: a chat window, a general user, a conversation that starts from zero. That's incredibly powerful for breadth, but it's structurally weak in depth. It doesn't own your codebase, your hospital's records, your supply chain, your legal workflow. It doesn't have the long-horizon context that accumulates in a real domain over months. And the super app can't easily go deep into every vertical without becoming something other than a super app.

That's where I think startups actually live now. The question isn't "can I build a chatbot," it's "can I own an environment where the agent has to operate, where the feedback signal is real, and where the data that comes out of using the product is something the model company doesn't have." If you own the environment, you own the evaluation. And in the current paradigm, whoever owns the evaluation effectively owns the ability to improve. That's hard for OpenAI to replicate from the chat box, because the chat box is generic by design.

The second thing I'd say is that the super app changes what "small" means. A lot of people think the only interesting companies are the ones that could become the next ChatGPT. But if ChatGPT is the browser, the interesting question is what gets built on top of or alongside the browser. Some of those things are large, some are not, but the structure of the opportunity is different: you're building for a world where general capability is a commodity you pull in, and the differentiation is in how you connect that capability to something real and messy.

The third thing, and this is maybe less comfortable, is that the super app really does raise the bar on taste. When capability is cheap, what's scarce is knowing which problem is worth solving and what the right evaluation for it is. I've said before that I think we're in a phase where defining the problem matters more than solving it, because the solving part is increasingly handled by models. A startup today is less about having a clever algorithm and more about having a very clear point of view on a domain, on what "good" looks like there, and on a loop that lets you keep improving faster than a generic product can.

So: fewer opportunities in the obvious places, more in the places where ChatGPT structurally can't go. And I think that's actually a healthier ecosystem than the one where everyone was building thin wrappers.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how ChatGPT changes startup opportunities, but does not state that adopting the super app reorganizes a company’s activities around it.

r002.rationale: It describes a different startup approach from ChatGPT: owning a domain environment, feedback and evaluation loop, rather than building a general chatbot or thin wrapper.

astra-6.text:
I think ChatGPT being a super app changes where startups can create value. If your product is something ChatGPT can offer directly—say, a general interface for asking questions or generating text—then you’re competing with a product that already has the user’s attention. Even if your feature is better today, distribution becomes a very difficult problem.

But there’s a difference between answering a question and actually doing someone’s work. In a particular industry, doing the work might require access to internal systems, understanding a complicated workflow, and being reliable enough that somebody will pay for the outcome. There’s a lot for a startup to build there beyond the model itself.

So I would ask: as ChatGPT gets better, does that make your company less necessary, or does it make your product more useful? If better models let you solve more of your customer’s problem, and you have the customer relationship and the workflow integration, then progress can be very good for you. The opportunity is to own a problem deeply enough that access to intelligence alone doesn’t solve it.

r001.rationale: The response says ChatGPT changes where startups can create value, but does not state that adopting the super app reorganizes a company's activities around it.

r002.rationale: It identifies opportunities in products that go beyond ChatGPT’s general question-answering interface: doing industry-specific work through internal systems and workflows, with reliable outcomes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think ChatGPT becoming a super app changes where startups can create value. If your product is something a user can get by asking ChatGPT one more question, then it’s hard to build a durable business around that. The platform already has the users, and improvements to the model may absorb what your product does.

But there’s a big gap between answering a question and doing someone’s work. A startup can focus on a particular workflow, connect to the systems people use, and take responsibility for getting a task completed. That requires more than intelligence. It requires context, integration, and a way to check whether the result is actually correct.

So I would look less at what ChatGPT cannot do today and more at what advantage you can keep as the models improve. Do you understand a customer’s problem much better? Do you have a way to learn from real usage? Can you reliably deliver an outcome people will pay for? In those cases, a stronger ChatGPT can also be good for you, because stronger underlying models make your product more capable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how ChatGPT shifts where startups can create value, but does not say a company reorganizes its activities around the super app.

r002.rationale: It contrasts ChatGPT answering questions with startups building workflow-focused products that integrate with systems and take responsibility for completing tasks.
